name: Tinia
role: Supreme Etruscan sky god and lord of lightning
fun_fact: Roman writers identified Tinia with Jupiter, and his three thunderbolts were later fitted into a system of eleven kinds of lightning.

name: Uni
role: Etruscan queen of the gods and patron of women and cities
fun_fact: At Pyrgi her sanctuary produced gold tablets in Etruscan and Phoenician that address her and Astarte in parallel.

name: Menerva
role: Etruscan goddess of wisdom, craft and war
fun_fact: Menerva was identified with Roman Minerva and shared the three-cella temple with Tinia and Uni, a plan Rome copied on the Capitoline.

name: Turms
role: Etruscan messenger god and guide of the dead
fun_fact: Inscriptions give the title Turms Aitas, Turms of the underworld, for the god who leads the dead.

name: Vanth
role: Winged Etruscan guide of the dead
fun_fact: Vanth often appears with a snake coiled around her arm and a scroll that may record the fate of the dead.

name: Charun
role: Etruscan death demon and guardian of the underworld
fun_fact: Despite the similar name, Etruscan Charun is not the ferryman of Greek myth but a hammer-wielding demon who guards the way to the underworld.

name: Tanaquil
role: Etruscan queen and interpreter of omens
fun_fact: Livy says she was skilled in celestial prodigies, and she used that skill to place her pupil Servius Tullius on the Roman throne.

name: Servius Tullius
role: Sixth king of Rome, raised in the Tarquin household
fun_fact: Roman tradition credits Servius with the census and the first city wall, while an Etruscan tomb at Vulci calls him Mastarna.

name: Haruspex
role: Etruscan diviner who read the gods' will in entrails and lightning
fun_fact: The Etruscan word for the office was netsvis, and Roman magistrates kept Etruscan haruspices on call for public prodigies.

name: Phersu
role: Masked figure in the Tomb of the Augurs at Tarquinia
fun_fact: The name Phersu is often linked to Latin persona, the word for a mask, but the connection is debated.
